app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:17 — rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` assigns a mutable array literal directly as a default property on an `Ember.Object` subclass rather than initializing it in `init`, a known Ember anti-pattern where the array instance would be shared across controller instances if this controller is ever instantiated more than once

goldens.comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.

The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:17 — rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` assigns a mutable array literal directly as a default property on an `Ember.Object` subclass rather than initializing it in `init`, a known Ember anti-pattern where the array instance would be shared across controller instances if this controller is ever instantiated more than once

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` as a default property on the controller class. In Ember, object/array default properties can be shared between instances because they’re created at class definition time rather than per-instance (typically done in `init`). While Discourse controllers are often singletons so it may not manifest as a user-facing defect, the finding is a concrete, diff-grounded concern about potential shared mutable state if multiple instances are ever created (e.g., tests, engine reuse, or non-standard instantiation).
